# Wirecard Public-Fraud Trail: Corporate Statements, Audit Uncertainty, Supervisory Failure, and Jan Marsalek

## Executive assessment

The evidence supplied supports a clear reconstruction of the public-fraud trail surrounding Wirecard, but it does not establish every element of the underlying criminal case. The strongest conclusion is that Wirecard’s public communications in April 2020 presented the KPMG investigation as having found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet manipulation, while the underlying investigation—as summarized in the European Parliament study—had not verified the existence or accuracy of major revenue streams and had been unable to locate or confirm approximately €1 billion in trust-account funds. Two months later, Wirecard acknowledged that approximately €1.9 billion in reported bank balances probably did not exist and filed for insolvency. This sequence creates a material contradiction between Wirecard’s public framing and the investigative uncertainty described in the later policy study. ([S1](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation); [S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The supplied evidence also supports the assessment that Wirecard’s collapse was not caused by one isolated control failure. The European Parliament study identifies failures across five lines of defence: Wirecard’s internal controls, its supervisory board, external auditing, financial-reporting and audit oversight bodies, and the German market supervisor BaFin. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)) However, the material provided does not establish that Jan Marsalek personally committed particular acts, nor does it provide a complete account of his disappearance. It only places him within the Wirecard leadership context and records a later German Federal Criminal Police Office public search for a responsible person. Any stronger statement would exceed the supplied evidence.

## Sources and evidentiary limitations

For clarity, this report uses two source IDs:

- **S1** — Wirecard AG’s 28 April 2020 regulatory announcement concerning delivery of the KPMG special-investigation report.
- **S2** — Langenbucher, Leuz, Kra hnen, and Pelizzon’s November 2020 European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit study, *What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?*

S1 is a contemporaneous company statement and therefore provides direct evidence of what Wirecard communicated to the market. It is not independent evidence that the company’s claims were true. S2 is a later analytical policy study commissioned by the European Parliament. It synthesizes public records and secondary sources, and expressly warns against hindsight bias. It is therefore valuable for reconstructing the institutional and chronological context, but it is not itself a criminal judgment or a final judicial determination of individual responsibility. ([S1](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation); [S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Chronology of the public-fraud trail

### Early warnings and critical information

The European Parliament study reports that concerns about Wirecard’s accounting practices existed for years before the company’s collapse. It identifies allegations dating back to 2008, including accusations by the shareholder association SdK that Wirecard reported unusually high margins and treated customer deposits as its own cash. It also refers to the 2016 Zatarra report, which accused Wirecard of corruption, fraud, and money laundering, while noting that some short-selling activity connected to Wirecard was itself investigated for possible market manipulation. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The Financial Times published a series of reports beginning in 2015 and later received internal documents from Wirecard employees in Singapore. The study characterizes these employees as whistleblowers concerned that an internal investigation had been suppressed. The evidence therefore indicates that information potentially relevant to Wirecard’s accounting and business practices was available outside the company before the 2020 collapse. It does not, however, establish that every allegation was accurate at the time it was made. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

### 2019 escalation

On 30 January 2019, the Financial Times reported allegations that Wirecard had used forged and backdated contracts to increase reported revenues. On 15 February, BaFin directed the German Financial Reporting Enforcement Panel, or FREP, to examine Wirecard’s interim group accounts as of 30 June 2018. On 18 February, BaFin prohibited the establishment or enlargement of net short positions in Wirecard shares until 18 April 2019, following approval by ESMA. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study’s assessment is critical of this intervention. It argues that a short-selling ban is asymmetric because it restricts negative information from being incorporated into market prices while leaving positive trading activity unaffected. The authors further argue that investors could have mistakenly interpreted the ban as a signal that BaFin possessed private information showing the short sellers were wrong. This is an expert assessment, not a judicial finding, but it is central to the report’s explanation of how market warnings may have been weakened. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

In October 2019, Wirecard hired KPMG to conduct a special forensic investigation into allegations reported in the press and elsewhere. The investigation was delayed, and Wirecard issued interim statements in March and April 2020 suggesting that no evidence of balance-sheet manipulation had been found so far. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## The April 2020 corporate statement and audit uncertainty

### What Wirecard said

On 28 April 2020, Wirecard announced that it had received KPMG’s special-investigation report. The company stated that “incriminating evidence” supporting public allegations of balance-sheet forgery had not been identified. It further stated that, across four areas—third-party acquiring, merchant cash advance/digital lending, India, and Singapore—KPMG had found no significant issues requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts. ([S1](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

Wirecard also stated that existing audit documentation and procedures had been sufficient to prove revenues in the third-party-acquiring business during the ordinary audits of 2016–2018. It acknowledged, however, that KPMG’s more demanding forensic requirements had not been satisfied by all available data because relevant information was primarily controlled by third parties. Wirecard emphasized that more than 200 million data records relating to December 2019 had been provided to KPMG and that this testing revealed no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. ([S1](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

The company also admitted documentation and organizational weaknesses, while presenting them as weaknesses already identified and being remedied through a Global Compliance Organization and external consultants. It postponed publication of its annual accounts and annual press conference, pending completion of audit measures with EY. ([S1](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

### What the later study reports about KPMG’s findings

S2 presents a materially more qualified account. It states that KPMG was unable to verify the existence of approximately €1 billion in foreign trust accounts and could neither confirm nor refute whether the third-party-acquiring revenues existed or were accurate in amount. The study quotes KPMG’s position that the available forensic work did not permit a conclusion either way regarding the existence and correctness of those revenues. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

This is not necessarily a direct logical contradiction if S1 is read narrowly. Wirecard said that KPMG had not identified “incriminating evidence” and that a separate data set from December 2019 showed no deviations. That does not necessarily mean that KPMG had positively verified every disputed 2016–2018 revenue stream or every trust-account balance. Nevertheless, Wirecard’s announcement could reasonably have conveyed a more reassuring impression than the underlying limitations described by S2.

The key evidentiary distinction is therefore:

| Issue | Wirecard statement | Later study’s account |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence of manipulation | No incriminating evidence identified | KPMG could not conclusively refute or confirm key allegations |
| TPA revenues | Existing audit measures were said to prove revenues; December 2019 data showed no deviations | KPMG could not determine whether relevant TPA revenues existed or were correct in amount |
| Trust-account funds | Not addressed in detail in S1 | Approximately €1 billion could not be verified |
| Internal weaknesses | Acknowledged, but described as being remedied | Treated as part of broader control and oversight failures |
| Annual reporting | Publication postponed | Delay became part of the wider escalation before insolvency |

The appropriate conclusion is not that S1 conclusively proves deliberate deception, because the supplied material does not provide a legal determination of that question. The stronger and supportable conclusion is that S1 presented a reassuring corporate interpretation of an investigation whose underlying evidentiary position remained substantially unresolved.

## Missing cash and collapse

The public trail changed decisively in June 2020. According to S2, on 22 June Wirecard’s board stated that bank balances of €1.9 billion held in trust accounts probably did not exist and that the third-party business might be incorrect in the manner previously described. On 25 June, Wirecard filed for insolvency because of impending insolvency and over-indebtedness. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The scale of the missing funds is significant. S2 describes €1.9 billion as equivalent to approximately one quarter of Wirecard’s balance sheet. The study also reports that EY refused to sign off the 2019 accounts after identifying forged bank confirmations and describing indications of a sophisticated fraud involving multiple parties and institutions. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

This progression supports a structured fraud-trail assessment:

1. Public allegations concerned revenue recognition, opaque third-party acquiring arrangements, and accounting inconsistencies.
2. Wirecard commissioned a forensic investigation and publicly emphasized the absence of incriminating findings.
3. The investigation nevertheless left major questions unresolved, especially concerning trust accounts and TPA revenues.
4. The company later acknowledged that €1.9 billion in reported bank balances probably did not exist.
5. EY declined to certify the 2019 accounts, and Wirecard entered insolvency proceedings.

The existence of missing cash is strongly supported by the supplied material. The precise mechanics by which the balances were reported, documented, transferred, or falsely confirmed remain incompletely established in these two sources.

## Audit and supervisory failures

### EY and audit limitations

S2 states that EY issued unqualified audit opinions for Wirecard’s 2015–2018 financial statements, despite serious public allegations. It reports that KPMG questioned both the verification of the trust accounts and whether their classification as cash or cash equivalents was appropriate under IFRS. S2 also reports allegations that EY relied on confirmations issued in the name of a trustee rather than independently confirming the underlying bank accounts. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study is careful to recognize that sophisticated fraud can be difficult to detect and that management and the supervisory board bear primary responsibility for preventing and detecting fraud. Nevertheless, it argues that auditors must obtain reasonable assurance that financial statements are free from material misstatement caused by fraud or error and must respond appropriately to indications of fraud. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

### FREP and BaFin

The German enforcement structure divided responsibility between FREP and BaFin. FREP conducted the first stage of financial-reporting examinations but depended substantially on voluntary cooperation. BaFin generally acted as the public enforcement authority after specified triggers, including non-cooperation or serious doubts about FREP’s conclusions. S2 argues that this two-step structure created delay, unclear responsibility, and weak accountability. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study further states that BaFin’s role was complicated because Wirecard’s parent company was not treated as a bank or financial holding company, even though the group included a bank subsidiary. As a result, BaFin did not have the full bank-supervisory powers that might have applied to a regulated banking entity. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The authors’ central assessment is that all five lines of defence failed in some way. Their recommended reforms included stronger auditor liability, mandatory effective internal controls, independent audit committees, expanded investigative powers for BaFin, a single public authority responsible for financial-reporting enforcement, and a potential European Single Capital Market Supervisor. These are policy recommendations, not evidence that the proposed institutions would necessarily have prevented the fraud. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Jan Marsalek and the limits of the supplied evidence

The requested target includes Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. The supplied sources do not provide a sufficiently detailed account to reconstruct it responsibly. S2 discusses the Wirecard leadership and includes a later reference to a Federal Criminal Police Office public search for a responsible person, but the excerpt does not provide a verified narrative of Marsalek’s movements, destination, assistance network, or legal status. It also does not establish that Marsalek alone directed or executed the alleged fraud. ([S2](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

Accordingly, the supportable conclusion is limited: Marsalek belongs to the public Wirecard fraud narrative as a senior company figure associated with the company’s collapse, but the two supplied sources are insufficient to attribute specific fraudulent acts to him or to explain his disappearance. Any account of his flight, location, intelligence connections, or post-disappearance activities would require additional sources and should not be inferred from this evidence set.

## Final findings

The supplied evidence supports the following concrete opinion:

> Wirecard’s public-fraud trail is best understood as a prolonged failure of verification and accountability rather than as a single late-stage accounting error. The company publicly characterized the April 2020 KPMG report as non-incriminating, but the available evidence at that point remained materially incomplete. The later discovery that €1.9 billion in reported trust-account balances probably did not exist transformed unresolved audit uncertainty into a confirmed corporate crisis. Weaknesses in internal controls, external auditing, financial-reporting enforcement, and market supervision allowed critical warnings to remain ineffective for too long. The evidence does not, however, permit a responsible conclusion about Jan Marsalek’s specific criminal conduct or disappearance beyond his relevance to the broader Wirecard leadership narrative.

## References

Langenbucher, K., Leuz, C., Kra hnen, J. P., & Pelizzon, L. (2020). *What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?* Economic Governance Support Unit, European Parliament. [https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

Wirecard AG. (2020, April 28). *Wirecard AG: KPMG delivers report on special investigation*. [https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)
